A team of United States scientists visited Ghana to support efforts to tackle mercury pollution linked to illegal small-scale gold mining and strengthen freshwater protection.
The delegation visited from November 7 to 21, bringing together specialists from the US Department of the Interior, the US Geological Survey (USGS) and the US Environmental Protection Agency.
Their work focused on water quality monitoring, mercury detection, laboratory capacity and sustainable mining practices.
The visit took place under the Ambassador’s Water Experts Program, a joint initiative of the US Departments of State and the Interior.
During consultations with Ghana’s Environmental Protection Agency, the experts discussed mercury contamination in freshwater systems affected by galamsey. They also examined the need for standardised testing methods and closer scientific collaboration.
The engagement builds on a 2024 baseline assessment by USGS scientist and former Embassy Science Fellow Dr Grace Armstrong. Her research identified elevated mercury levels in the waters and sediments of the Pra and Ankobra river systems.
“The challenges posed by mercury pollution require coordinated scientific approaches and trusted partnerships,” she said.
“Our work together helps ensure that data collected in Ghana meets rigorous standards and supports effective decision-making for environmental protection.”
A two-day symposium on November 10 and 11 brought together US and Ghanaian experts, civil society organisations, academics and industry representatives.
Held under the theme, “Addressing Mercury Pollution: Collaborative Solutions for Sustainable Mining in Ghana,” it examined the environmental, health and security effects of mercury use. Participants also explored practical and commercially viable mercury-free mining technologies.
Speaking at the symposium, then US Chargé d’Affaires Rolf Olson said protecting freshwater resources was critical to Ghana’s future.
“Protecting Ghana’s freshwater resources is essential not only for environmental and public health, but also for long-term economic and food security,” he said.
“The United States is committed to working with Ghana to strengthen scientific capacity, advance responsible mining practices, and promote American technological solutions that support sustainable development.”
US Environmental Protection Agency expert Dr Chris Eckley also highlighted the potential value of sharing technical experience.
“Drawing on U.S. experience assessing and remediating mercury-contaminated sites could help our Ghanaian counterparts address local environmental challenges,” he said.
The delegation engaged students, researchers, civil society organisations and youth groups on water protection, training and field research.
Participating institutions included the University of Ghana, Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology, the University of Environment and Sustainable Development, and Accra STEM Academy.
The exchanges aimed to improve the reliability of laboratory analyses and support the adoption of international best practices in water-quality monitoring and mercury detection.
